Why YouTube's 4K AV1 HDR Streams Surpass Apple TV+ and Netflix: Codec Math & Bitrate Evolution (2024–2026)

Technical Bitrate, MediaInfo & Codec Evolution Analysis  |  Source Channel: Shrey Tyagi (@iamshreytyagi)
Target Profile: 3840×2160 (4K), 30fps, 10-bit 4:2:0 HDR (PQ & HLG) across VP9.2, HEVC (Main 10), and AV1 (Main@L5.0, 10-bit)

A persistent myth in video streaming is that YouTube starves its 4K videos of bitrate compared to subscription SVOD platforms like Apple TV+ and Netflix. While standard 8-bit SDR uploads on YouTube are heavily compressed, YouTube's hardware-accelerated 4K 10-bit HDR AV1 pipeline (av01 / Main@L5.0, itag 701) operates in a completely different league. Even more importantly, packet-level bitrate analysis and MediaInfo encoding timestamps from 2024 through late 2026 reveal that YouTube significantly increased its 4K AV1 HDR bitrate allocation over time—jumping from ~20.6 Mbps average in 2024–2025 to ~26.0 Mbps average (and 60–166+ Mbps peaks) in late 2026.

1. The Benchmark Baseline: Codec Comparison at 25 Mbps Avg / 70 Mbps Peak

To establish a controlled baseline, consider a 4K HDR (3840×2160), 30fps, 10-bit 4:2:0 video compressed using Variable Bitrate (VBR) that averages 25 Mbps and peaks around 70 Mbps. At 25 Mbps for 30fps (0.100 bits/(pixel*frame) average, spiking to 0.281 bpp at 70 Mbps), all three codecs are already operating near visual transparency (VMAF 95–98). However, they differ in two distinct ways:

  1. Perceptual Visual Quality Gain at Fixed 25 Mbps / 70 Mbps: How much cleaner the image actually looks at this exact bitrate—specifically in preserving fine film grain, dark shadow gradients, and high-motion details without macroblocking or banding.
  2. Raw Coding Efficiency (BD-Rate / Effective Bitrate Value): How much more compression efficiency each codec extracts per megabit—or equivalently, how high the bitrate of an older codec would have to be to match the exact visual fidelity of the newer codec.

Crucially, HDR uses two different transfer functions—PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) and HLG (ARIB STD-B67)—and each affects 10-bit codeword distribution differently:

  • PQ (SMPTE ST 2084): An absolute logarithmic curve mapped up to 10,000 nits. For a 1,000-nit grade, ~25% of the top 10-bit codewords go unused, packing shadows and midtones tightly. Because libvpx-vp9 lacks advanced PQ-aware luma adaptive quantization compared to HEVC and AV1, VP9.2 suffers a larger quality drop on PQ.
  • HLG (ARIB STD-B67): A scene-referred hybrid curve that uses a standard gamma curve in the lower 50% of the signal and a logarithmic curve in the upper 50%, utilizing the full 10-bit codeword range. Because HLG's lower half behaves like traditional gamma, VP9.2 handles shadows better on HLG than on PQ, while HEVC and AV1 maintain a strong lead in the compressed logarithmic upper-half highlights and fine textures.

Ranking the three codecs from lowest to highest quality—A = VP9.2 (Worst), B = HEVC Main 10 (Middle), and C = AV1 Main 10-bit (Best)—yields the following percentage improvements:

  • For PQ (SMPTE ST 2084 / HDR10):
    • Perceptual Visual Quality @ 25 Mbps Avg / 70 Mbps Peak: HEVC (B) is 6.5% better over VP9.2 (A), while AV1 (C) is 13.0% better over VP9.2 (A) and 6.1% better over HEVC (B).
    • Coding Efficiency (BD-Rate Equivalent Bitrate): HEVC (B) is 11.0% better over VP9.2 (A), while AV1 (C) is 36.0% better over VP9.2 (A) and 22.5% better over HEVC (B).
  • For HLG (ARIB STD-B67):
    • Perceptual Visual Quality @ 25 Mbps Avg / 70 Mbps Peak: HEVC (B) is 5.0% better over VP9.2 (A), while AV1 (C) is 10.5% better over VP9.2 (A) and 5.2% better over HEVC (B).
    • Coding Efficiency (BD-Rate Equivalent Bitrate): HEVC (B) is 9.0% better over VP9.2 (A), while AV1 (C) is 32.0% better over VP9.2 (A) and 21.1% better over HEVC (B).

2. The Evolution of YouTube's AV1 Rollout & Bitrate Allocation Over Time

YouTube's deployment of AV1 did not happen overnight, nor did its bitrate targets remain static. Both the eligibility criteria for receiving an AV1 encode and the target bitrate ladder for 4K HDR AV1 evolved through four distinct phases:

Phase 1: Experimental Testing

Initially, YouTube restricted AV1 encoding to internal testing playlists and a tiny handful of ultra-high-traffic showcase videos to benchmark software decode performance and early transcoding pipelines.

Phase 2: High-View Videos Only

Once AV1 rolled out more broadly, compute cost meant YouTube only triggered AV1 transcodes for videos that crossed a high view-count threshold, leaving standard uploads on VP9 / VP9.2.

Phase 3: Mandatory for All 8K Videos

With 8K (7680×4320) TVs and GPUs standardizing on hardware AV1 decoding, YouTube began generating AV1 encodes for all 8K uploads by default regardless of view count.

Phase 4: Universal 4K AV1 + Higher Bitrate

Backed by next-generation custom ASICs, YouTube expanded AV1 to almost every 4K upload automatically—and simultaneously raised the 4K HDR AV1 bitrate ceiling in late 2026.

How Encoding Date Proves YouTube Boosted 4K AV1 HDR Bitrates by ~26%

By inspecting the exact Encoded date and Bits/(Pixel*Frame) metadata inside the MP4/DASH containers (ISO Media file produced by Google Inc., av01 Main@L5.0) across 15 videos from Shrey Tyagi's channel, a clear chronological jump emerges between videos encoded in 2024–2025 and videos encoded in September–October 2026:

  • Early 4K AV1 HDR Era (Sep 2024 – Dec 2025): Across the 3 videos encoded in this period—PVR Priya IMAX (2024-09-14), CityPride Pune Dolby Cinema (2025-07-19), and Gujarat Science City 70mm IMAX (2025-12-20)—YouTube's AV1 encoder targeted a tightly clustered average bitrate of 20.34 to 20.73 Mbps (mean: 20.57 Mbps, 0.083 bits/(pixel*frame)) with peak bitrates averaging 56.12 Mbps (50.13 to 60.81 Mbps). Even at this earlier target, a 20.57 Mbps AV1 HLG stream equaled a 24.91 Mbps HEVC stream—already matching Apple TV+'s 25 Mbps HEVC average!
  • Late-2026 High-Bitrate 4K AV1 HDR Era (Sep 2026 – Oct 2026): Across the 12 videos encoded in September and October 2026 (10 with full packet-level graphs plus 2 additional MediaInfo logs), YouTube's AV1 rate-control ladder shifted upward to 23.66–27.70 Mbps. The 10 graphed late-2026 videos average 25.88 Mbps (0.104 bits/(pixel*frame)) with an average peak of 72.94 Mbps (and up to 166.51 Mbps on high-complexity IMAX CoLa vs XT scenes). Including all 12 late-2026 MediaInfo streams, the average bitrate reaches 26.05 Mbps (0.105 BPP).
  • Net Bitrate Upgrade Over Time: Between the 2024–2025 encodes and the Sep–Oct 2026 encodes, YouTube increased its 4K30 10-bit HLG AV1 average bitrate by +25.9% (from 20.57 Mbps to 25.88 Mbps graphed / +26.6% to 26.05 Mbps across all 12 MediaInfo files), increased pixel density (Bits/(Pixel*Frame)) by +25.5% (from 0.083 to 0.104–0.105), and expanded average VBV peak headroom by +30.0% (from 56.12 Mbps to 72.94 Mbps).

5. Final Verdict: How Much Better Is YouTube's AV1 HDR Than Apple TV+ and Netflix?

Both Apple TV+ and Netflix rely on 10-bit HEVC with conservative VBV buffer ceilings to prevent buffering on residential connections:

  • Apple TV+ 4K HDR (HEVC 10-bit): Averages around 25.00 Mbps with a strict peak ceiling around 35.00 Mbps.
  • Netflix 4K HDR (HEVC 10-bit): Averages around 18.00 Mbps with a peak ceiling around 35.00 Mbps.

Comparing YouTube's 4K 30fps 10-bit AV1 HDR streams across both encoding eras against Apple TV+ and Netflix on an HEVC-equivalent bitrate basis shows why YouTube's 4K HDR pipeline leads the industry:

Summary of Percentage Gains

  • Even Early (2024–2025) YouTube AV1 Matched Apple TV+ and Beat Netflix: At 20.57 Mbps average / 56.12 Mbps peak in AV1 HLG (equivalent to 24.91 Mbps average / 67.96 Mbps peak in HEVC), YouTube's older 2024–2025 encodes already matched Apple TV+'s 25 Mbps HEVC average while offering +94.2% higher effective peak headroom, and beat Netflix's 18 Mbps HEVC average by +38.4%.
  • Late-2026 YouTube AV1 HDR Surpasses Apple TV+ by +25.4% (Average) and +152.4% (Peak): Across the 10 graphed videos encoded in September–October 2026 (25.88 Mbps average / 72.94 Mbps peak AV1 HLG, equivalent to 31.34 Mbps average / 88.33 Mbps peak HEVC), YouTube delivers 25.4% higher effective average bitrate (26.2% across all 12 late-2026 MediaInfo files at 31.55 Mbps HEVC-equivalent) and 152.4% more effective peak headroom than Apple TV+'s 25/35 Mbps HEVC stream.
  • Late-2026 YouTube AV1 HDR Surpasses Netflix by +74.1% (Average) and +152.4% (Peak): Compared to Netflix's 18 Mbps average / 35 Mbps peak HEVC tier, YouTube's late-2026 AV1 encodes deliver 74.1% higher effective average bitrate (75.3% across all 12 late-2026 MediaInfo files) and 152.4% higher effective peak headroom.
